title: Ferrari drivers 'here to attack' in Singapore GP
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton insists that he and Ferrari team mate Charles Leclerc are "here to attack" during the Singapore Grand Prix this weekend.

Hamilton arrives after a fightback drive last time out in Malaysia, where the wrong tyre strategy initially on a wet track meant the seven-time World Champion had to claw his way back to the podium from towards the rear of the field.

It was the first podium for Hamilton since the British Grand Prix back in July, with the Briton insisting on Thursday's media day in Singapore that the result last weekend did not necessarily mean Ferrari were back in contention for victory.

"It's not that we come here with momentum, we've had one good race last weekend and we'll try and build on that," said Hamilton.

"I think this should be an okay circuit for us, there's lots of challenges, particularly that it's a Sprint weekend, which makes this track the most challenging of the year. We're just going over the numbers and trying to make sure we start in the right place."

He added: "I've been pushing the car in a certain direction and I think we are slowly making gains and improvements. We're here to attack, Qualifying is key and it would be really great if we could start tomorrow on the right foot and then just attacking in Qualifying."

Despite a poor run of form over the last few events, Hamilton was hopeful that Ferrari's 2026 challenger would be better suited to Singapore's street venue, where a high downforce setup would be required.

"I think with our car it's generally good on street circuits, particularly when there's not long straights. If you look at the last races we're quick through corners, not so quick in a straight line," he said.

"This is a high drag circuit, so I'm hoping that the advantage others have on those long straights comes down a little bit and we can start matching them through corners."

Team mate Leclerc was cautious, however, believing that Ferrari may have slipped down in the performance pecking order, with the team's place as Mercedes' nearest opposition having been taken by McLaren and Red Bull in recent races.

"Historically we've been quite strong here, but we cannot really rely on the past," said Leclerc.

"We've got to do everything we can in order to be in the best possible situation. It's also true that the tendency lately has been that we're losing a bit of performance compared to the guys in front, so to win will be very difficult."

title: Verstappen evaluates chances of long-awaited Singapore win
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has insisted that he’s “going to try” to secure his first win at the Singapore Grand Prix, but remains aware that even after his victory in Malaysia, “there are no guarantees” due to the tight competition at the front of the field.

Following a frustrating start to the 2026 season, Verstappen finally returned to the top step last time out at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, where he beat Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli and Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton.

Although the achievement suggested that Red Bull might be able to fight for wins regularly, the Dutchman explained that it would be “complicated” to do so at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, especially as his best result there was a trio of P2 finishes in 2025, 2024 and 2018.

Quizzed on whether he’s now in a place to chase down that long-awaited win in Singapore, he replied: “We're going to try, that's for sure. It's always complicated on a street circuit, a lot of things have to come together.

“Some just happen a bit sooner than others and unfortunately for a lot of different reasons, we have not won here yet, even in our dominant years.

“But you always need to look at the strengths of the car and Singapore was a track where our car didn't really come alive before. I hope it's going to be a little bit better this year but there are no guarantees.

“There are a lot of other teams that are also very strong on street circuits and also every street circuit is very different. This is not like Baku, for example, and it's also not like Monaco. We'll see.”

With seven rounds of the season remaining, Verstappen went on to explain that he wants to stay realistic about Red Bull’s chances and set just one goal – to seal another win before they shift their focus to 2027.

“I just want to try and see if we can carry this momentum and try to be in a position again to win potentially,” he said. “I don't know if that's here or in another race.

“We have won one race finally and then we also need to stay with two feet on the ground and keep working because I'm sure that it's not always going to be like this now until the end of the season. Step by step we try to be better and next year is a completely different story.”

Verstappen’s triumph in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia would’ve been made even sweeter by a double podium for the team, and while Isack Hadjar came close, a battery issue dropped him to P5 late on.

Reflecting on the weekend, Hadjar said: “To be honest, it's still an ongoing analysis, but at the same time, I don't think whatever happened in Malaysia is going to impact us heading into Singapore.

“But still, I'm not the type of guy who just moves on anyway, ‘ah, the race is finished’. I want everything to be understood and, even if now I'm focused on Singapore, I am happy to then come back into a bit more details.”

It was nevertheless a strong showing by the Frenchman, who was able to celebrate a historic first win for Red Bull Ford Powertrains just two races into his return from injury.

“[When] we started in Melbourne, I was like nine-tenths behind Mercedes in third. And then we kind of went downhill, so at some point we were even further away from the leaders, and from then we kind of managed to reach decent results, had some form, average form.

“I would say it was kind of a plateau for a bit of the European period, and then that final upgrade kind of put us in contention, and also you have Max in the car so it kind of helps. It's great to have a Red Bull power unit win a race. They've been doing that for only four years and they won an F1 race already, so it's impressive.”

title: Mercedes will 'find an answer' to unlocking upgrades – Antonelli
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli believes that Mercedes can “find an answer” as to why their most recent upgrades haven’t delivered the intended performance boost, with the Italian set to run a new front wing designed to complement the package in Singapore.

While rival teams such as Ferrari and Red Bull introduced fairly regular updates over the season, Mercedes opted to wait until the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to make major changes to their challenger, including altered bodywork and adjustments to the floor.

They had hoped that these would reinstate the performance advantage they enjoyed earlier in the season, but that didn’t quite come to fruition. Instead, Red Bull’s Max Verstappen converted pole position into a win for the first time in 2026, while George Russell retired due to a mechanical issue.

Although Antonelli still finished on the podium behind Verstappen, the race showed that Mercedes have work to do in order to optimise their current package over the remaining rounds.

Asked whether a new front wing will help the upgrades to perform as they should, Antonelli responded: “That's the question we will try to answer. George is going back on the old package, which we know works really well, especially on these kinds of tracks.

“On my side, we'll try to find an answer for this package. Hopefully we will understand it more and finally strike the potential of the package. Of course we'll have the front wing, even though it's just one front wing, but let's see.

“I think Sepang overall was a little bit of an outlier because of the tarmac, the high temperatures, but hopefully this weekend we will be able to put the car in a better place and just extract more out of the package.”

Alongside reverting to a previous specification, Russell will also receive a significant grid penalty for exceeding his power unit allocation, giving Antonelli an opportunity to further increase his advantage in the drivers’ standings.

He currently leads his team mate by 84 points, but insisted that his attention remains on working to get the most out of Mercedes’ upgrades rather than thinking about the ongoing battle against Russell.

“I've committed with the new package and I will commit for the whole weekend,” he said. “There's no way to go back to it because it's a big job for the team.

“We will try to do the best with what we have but I'm more confident coming to this weekend because I feel like hopefully we will have a better understanding of the package and we will be able to extract more of its potential.

“We're going to try and win. That's the mindset and of course, George is starting at the back but it doesn't mean anything. On my side I just try to focus on what I can control and try to deliver the best performance as I can and if I can win the race, great.

“If I have to do a podium, I will do a podium. I'm really looking forward to the weekend and hopefully we can achieve a great result with the team.”

title: Russell promises ‘all-out attack’ in Singapore amid penalty
excerpt:
George Russell has promised an “all-out attack” in the Singapore Grand Prix as he prepares to line up at the back of the grid thanks to an engine-related penalty.

Russell has been forced to take on new power unit components following his late-race retirement at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last time out, which cost him valuable championship points.

The subsequent penalty will be a minimum of 10 positions depending on the exact parts Mercedes switch out, and how many of his allowances for the season that he exceeds.

As per the regulations, the first time the allocation of any one of the elements is exceeded, a 10-place grid penalty will be applied, with the second time this occurs (and so on) resulting in a five-place grid drop – all penalties at the same event applying in a cumulative manner.

If a driver incurs a penalty exceeding 15 grid places, they will be required to start the race at the back of the field regardless.

Asked about his mindset and approach arriving in Singapore, with the grid penalty hanging over him, Russell said: “All-out attack; just trying to enjoy the weekend.

“Obviously, if you could choose where to take the penalty in the season, this [track] would be probably the second bottom of the list after Monaco. But unfortunately, just with how things have panned out, we have no choice but to take it here.

“Also, because it’s so early, we’ve still got seven races to go, we’ll probably have to take another one down the line as well, so it’s obviously not an ideal situation. But Singapore is a place I love, and I’ll try and carve my way through the pack.”

Another topic of note for Mercedes heading into the Marina Bay event is the team’s plan to run old and new versions of their W17 challenger – championship leader Kimi Antonelli due to press on with the latest updates, and Russell set to revert to the package he drove to pole position and victory in Azerbaijan.

“It is back,” said Russell of his previous specification car, given the question marks over Mercedes’ upgrades at Sepang. “Obviously Malaysia was the worst weekend of the year for us as a team, in terms of pace, Qualifying result.

“Of course, we probably both would have been on the podium, but it was a difficult one, and we don’t know whether that was Malaysia specific or whether that was anything to do with the upgrade.

“There are no major signs telling us it’s anything to do with the upgrade, but we don’t measure performance in F1 on how much downforce a car produces. You measure it with a stopwatch, and the stopwatch wasn’t great in Malaysia, so let’s see this weekend.

“I’m very happy to be back on that package and do the compare, and I’m not really in any sort of fight this weekend, or the championship for that regard, so it’s the right place to do it.”

Russell’s penalty will be applied for Sunday’s Singapore Grand Prix, rather than Saturday’s Sprint, in which eight points are up for grabs.

title: Norris ‘hopeful’ recent car issue will be cured in Singapore
excerpt:
Lando Norris has offered an honest assessment of McLaren’s last two race weekends, stating that he and the team have “underperformed” and “need to do a better job” moving forward.

Boosted by mid-season updates, Norris charged to three out of four pole positions, and two race victories, across the Budapest, Zandvoort, Monza and Madrid rounds – raising McLaren’s hopes for the final phase of the campaign.

However, the last two events at Baku and Sepang served as a reality check for the Woking-based team, with neither Norris nor team mate Oscar Piastri making it onto the podium, and the Briton being plagued by unspecified straight-line speed issues.

At the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Red Bull, Mercedes and Ferrari all appeared to have superior raw pace, leaving McLaren to scratch their heads and come up with some answers ahead of this weekend’s visit to Singapore.

Asked about the learnings from Sepang during Thursday’s media activities at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, Norris said: “Oh, there were a fair few, both from my side, and from us as a team. Obviously from what happened in the race, but also just general things from a car point of view and what we need to do a better job in, and how can we get back to the same level as we were in the previous few: Budapest, Zandvoort and Madrid.

“So, the team have been working very hard, we’ve all worked very hard to understand what we could learn from last weekend, what we can and need to do better in. The exact things, the specifics of it, I don’t need to go into, but there was a good amount.

“There were some obvious ones, such as the straight-line speed, and the issues I’ve been having with the car, and obviously more technical ones, [like] how can we unlock more potential from the car to get back to the performance that we had previously. That’s a tricky one to do.”

As for whether some of McLaren’s deficit at Sepang was track-specific, Norris continued: “Well, at Baku we weren’t necessarily too quick either, so I wouldn’t say just a Malaysia thing. There are certainly some aspects of Malaysia, with the roughness of the tarmac, that we think does play a part.

“It’s a good thing for us to see this weekend if some of the performance that we were missing there does come back. Singapore is a track I’ve enjoyed, and we’ve been pretty good here over the last few years.

“Certainly, a little bit of it is track layout, and the last couple of tracks have not been to the same strengths as what we’ve seen in Madrid and some of the other races, but all in all we’ve still been underperforming to the level we need to and we want to be, so we still need to do a better job no matter what.”

Norris was then asked about the work McLaren have been carrying out in a bid to get on top of the specific straight-line speed issue he has been facing over the last couple of events, with the Briton “hopeful” things will be back to normal this time out.

“We need to get it on track first and see how much better [it is],” added Norris, who claimed pole and the race win in Singapore in 2024, as well as podium finishes in 2023 and 2025. “It’s obviously also a circuit where straight lines are not like the highest priority, and not as detrimental as the last few weekends.

“Nevertheless, you always want to go down the straights as quickly as what you should be able to. It’s always tough when you come out of corners better and end up going slower. It’s been a frustrating two weekends trying to figure out what the issue has been and why there’s just been a constant lack of straight-line speed and performance.

“Especially in this kind of battle we’ve been in [at the front of the grid], the last two Qualifyings it’s been [a difference of] two or three positions, so it’s cost me quite a lot. At the same time, there’s obviously things I can do better as well.

“I’m confident that the team have done a good job. They’ve put a lot of work into trying to figure out things. I’m hopeful that it will be better this weekend, but honestly I have to get out on track and see first.”

McLaren head into the Singapore weekend holding third position in the Teams’ Championship standings on 316 points, behind Ferrari on 405 and leaders Mercedes on 556, and just 18 points ahead of fourth-placed Red Bull.

title: Verstappen answers your questions in our exclusive Q&A
excerpt:
This weekend, Max Verstappen will celebrate his 250th Grand Prix on the streets of Singapore, bringing another milestone in the Dutchman’s trophy-filled F1 career that began just over a decade ago.

To mark the special occasion, F1.com recently sat down with the four-time World Champion and put your questions to him – topics spanning his F1 journey, off-track interests, future goals and much more.

So, without further ado, read on (or watch) below to find out if your question made it into Verstappen’s bag of fan mail, and what he said in response…

Emma, UK: What is the best advice someone ever gave you that helped you in many areas of your life?

Just be yourself! Stay with two feet on the ground. I think that’s the most important.

Andy, Canada: The 2024 Sao Paulo race was the gutsiest thing I have seen with you racing in the rain. What was going through your mind with almost zero visibility at those speeds? My teeth hurt from clenching when I watched it. Best race I have ever seen…

Well, I mean, I had another race in Sao Paulo in 2016 that was probably… I would say even worse in terms of visibility at times. But yeah, it’s just… You’ve practiced a lot in your life driving in the wet in general, like racing in the rain. Yeah, the visibility at times is not great, but it’s the same for everyone, so you just have to deal with it. But for sure it was an insane race, and for me at the time, of course, a very important one to win.

Alexandra, Ukraine: Which F1 driver would you trust the most to babysit your cats?

Probably Alex Albon, because he has cats himself, like quite a few, so he definitely knows what to do!

Evan, Norway: What’s a hobby you've picked up that surprised you?

Well, I started playing padel like a few years ago now. I never really played any kind of racket sport before, so I didn’t know that that was on the horizon, but I enjoy it a lot.

Nancy, Canada: What is the best part of being a new dad?

The best part… I mean, just spending time with her and seeing her grow, seeing that it’s your little girl. That’s definitely the best part of it.

Nia Anand, Singapore: If all the F1 drivers on the grid were stuck in an airport overnight, who would solve the problem? Who would make it worse? And where would you be?

Well, who would solve the problem… I would solve the problem! Who would it make it worse? Who would make it worse, my God… Let’s just not get stuck in the airport, probably. I don’t know. I have no idea who would actually make it worse, because when you’re stuck in an airport that’s already, I guess, ‘worse’ enough. I don’t know what can be worse. If you’re stuck in an airport, what can you make worse? And where would I be? Where would I be? Well, stuck at the airport!

Robert, UK: If you were not racing in any form of motorsport, what would you be doing for a job?

I would still, I think, work in motorsport, but probably more in like a manager role or trying to just advise young talents – if I wouldn’t have succeeded in F1.

Lia, Ukraine: Looking back on your first 249 Grands Prix, which race taught you the biggest lesson?

It’s hard to pinpoint. I mean, to pick out one specific race, it’s just… Life, I guess, is a lesson, your career as well, your races, good and bad. You learn from every single race, some a little bit more than others. I think it’s just taking the general experience, and that probably makes you a better driver. It’s hard to just pick one particular race.

Cian, Ireland: If F1 had two-seater cars, who are you bringing into the cockpit and why?

Probably family members, friends… close friends and family members. I would not just take one person.

Verena, the Netherlands: What are some important values you have and live by, that help you be as successful as you are in F1 and in life?

Trying to live it as relaxed as possible, not really caring too much about stuff, social media… Just live your life normally, happy, with the people that you want to live it with. Try to keep it just very simple: keep life very simple.

Jaquavius, Brazil: What is your favourite food?

Good name! Tomato soup and beef carpaccio.

Ava, Australia: Which driver has challenged you the most in your career, on and off the track?

Which driver? It’s hard. It’s hard to pick one. I mean, in F1, of course, you have a lot of great drivers. I had a lot great team mates in go-karting. You learn from all of your team mates, for example, over your career… different things. I think it’s just the general experience of having your team mates challenge you, other drivers challenge you. It’s hard to just pick one particular person, I would say.

Prathik, India: Do you miss being Daniel Ricciardo’s team mate?

Yeah, well, I miss my times with Daniel, for sure. He’s a great guy. Sometimes we still catch up a little bit. Yeah, looking back at it, it was definitely a really fun period of my career also, with him. It’s definitely… When we see each other, we talk about it and have a good laugh.

Mina, Slovenia: What’s your favourite way to relax after a race weekend?

My favourite way to relax is probably just going home and spending time with my family, with the kids, just not thinking about racing too much.

Ibrahim, Australia: Have you ever lost hope at a certain point in your career? And if you have, how did you handle it?

No, I’ve not lost hope. I mean, you just need to keep trying to work towards your goal, and it’s not always an upwards trend or like a straight line. If you’re very passionate about what you do, and you love what you’re doing, you just keep going at it, and some days are better than others.

Alice, Czech Republic: What do you want your legacy to be?

Uhm, what do I want my legacy to be? As long as, I think, people can remember me as just being honest, straightforward, and always being myself, not trying to act like a different person suddenly… For me, that’s the most important, just to be remembered exactly like I am.

Joseph, USA: If you could have dinner with any F1 legend to discuss the sport or life, who would it be?

I never really had those kind of things [wishes]. I don’t want to meet anyone famous. I just want to spend time with my friends and family when I can, and that will be the best dinner anyway! Just with the people that you love, you have a great time, you laugh a lot, so I never really had the urge or desire to have dinner with someone that I don’t know.

Dana, Belgium: If you could say something to your little ‘you’ (when you were a child), what would you say?

I would say nothing. I would just let him live his life, experience the good things, the bad things, because at the end of the day, it all helps you to become a better driver, a better person. If you know everything in advance, probably life is very boring...

Maka Penny, Peru: Outside of the racing world, what’s something you still hope to achieve or build in your lifetime?

Travel the world more, spend time with my family and friends. It’s not really about achieving or building, it’s actually spending time with the people that you miss a lot throughout your F1 career.

Arek, Poland: If you could freely choose (from both current and past) one track, one car and one opponent to race against, what and who would you pick?

Spa, early 2000s F1 cars, maybe like 2004, and my dad.

Azra, Cyprus: What was your childhood nickname, if you had any?

I didn’t have any, because my name is nice and short! Max is very easy.

title: ‘Chill’ snakes and a 420km journey – Bottas’ epic bike ride
excerpt:
While most of the Formula 1 paddock travelled directly from Malaysia to Singapore after last weekend's race in Sepang, Valtteri Bottas chose a very different route.

Rather than taking the short hop from Kuala Lumpur to Singapore by plane for the next round of the season at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, Cadillac's Bottas opted to cover the distance by bicycle over several days.

The Finn made it safely to Singapore following his epic trip and, unsurprisingly, his adventure was one of the main talking points during Thursday's media day in the paddock.

"I'm really glad I did it because I saw pretty much the whole of Malaysia in a few days and the wild side of it, like the jungles, the plantations, bit of riding at night as well," he told the media in Singapore.

"Happy to be here safe and [it] all went as expected."

Bottas' Malaysian adventure

Bottas' adventure on two wheels began just hours after the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia concluded, a race in which he spun out and failed to finish. That evening, the Finn travelled 56.60km from Kuala Lumpur to Port Dickson, a journey that took him just over two hours.

On Monday, he spent almost six hours in the saddle, covering a mammoth 161.91km via Malacca City before reaching Muar. Bottas then continued south on Tuesday, spending more than five hours on the road while covering another 161km, before heading along the coast on natural paths and the gravelled, less common roads of the country.

Eventually the 10-time race winner made it from the coast to Batu Pahat, and then through Senggarang, a town whose name is linked to a local crocodile legend.

His route continued further away from the coast, riding through Kelapa Sawit before reaching his final destination of the day, Kulai.

On Wednesday, he put in a 'slightly' shorter leg and, after a total journey of 419.67km, arrived in Singapore.

While the ride was a considerable undertaking, Bottas said it would not affect his preparations for the weekend.

"Everything was really well planned," he reassured people on Thursday. "The distances for each day [were] planned so that I can recover for the weekend.

"So yesterday ended up being quite a short day, almost like a recovery day. Today is an easy day and it's those distances, not really unusual for me. I do long rides every now and then and I know how I can recover.

"And surely now I'm used to the heat, I was sweating a lot and I think day-by-day you start to feel better in the heat."

A familiar pursuit away from F1

Bottas is no stranger to life on two wheels. Earlier this year he secured a place at the Gravel World Championships by finishing fifth in his age group at a qualifying event in the Czech Republic. However, the championship takes place this weekend, ruling out his participation as he competes in the Singapore Grand Prix.

He doesn't have any more odysseys planned for the near future, though – but never say never.

"Sometimes you just have to jump into things," he said. "You have to just go for it and this is what I did. It sounded a little bit like a crazy idea but actually ended up being absolutely fine."

And there was one big bonus to top it all, he concluded.

"I overcame some of my little fears, I think, because I don't really like snakes but I saw a couple and they were really chill!"

title: Why Aston Martin expect another strong weekend in Singapore
excerpt:
Aston Martin enjoyed their strongest weekend of the 2026 season in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia with Fernando Alonso’s storming drive to eighth place, and the hopes are high for another positive week to come.

Chief Trackside Officer Mike Krack says the team are now “quite confident” that they can have another good showing in Singapore. There’s a simple reason for that – the Marina Bay layout has fewer long straights and is less power dependent that some of the tracks that preceded Sepang, and also some of those coming up.

"I think this is a track that should suit us decently,” he said on Thursday. “And it's also a Sprint, which brings its challenges as well. We have the weather unknown always here, so I think it can be an opportunity.

“But you must not do any mistakes. You know that I'm preaching always the same things, because they are always applying. But we are quite confident for this weekend.”

As Krack hinted, the Sprint format also will add an element of randomness with the lack of time to get the set-up right: “I think Fernando was first here last year in FP1, and was fourth in FP2, and we did not have the fourth car or the first car.

“So I think this is a track when you have to go into Qualifying, you have not much practice before. You have to get it right straight away. There are not many support series, so the track will evolve a lot.”

The layout aside, Krack conceded that the abrasive surface in Sepang also contributed to the good result.

“We have obviously looked into it, and we know the strength and the weaknesses of our package,” he said. “What could have happened is that the track was really an outlier in terms of surface. The surface roughness was very high, and with that the grip is low, and the time where you are grip limited is increasing and you move everything to lower speed.

“Now, the car is quite strong in these sections, so I think this helped us in terms of competitivity. I think also maybe other manufacturers had some issues, so I think it's a combination of both.”

Meanwhile, the team arrived in Singapore with the entire squad boosted by the strong Sepang race after a run of retirements and uncompetitive outings.

“Yeah, definitely there is there is a big boost all week,” said Krack. “We travelled together obviously straight away after Malaysia to come here, and then over the over the first days Monday and Tuesday you could see it's a relief – it has been a relief to score good points, and this will help everybody. And now coming to Singapore, we are motivated to continue.”

So can Krack see a change in Alonso when he has a sniff of a good result?

“He's one of these drivers that if there is a chance, he will not miss it,” he said. “You can feel it in the way we do the debriefs, in the way we ask questions, you can see he feels that something is possible. It's difficult to describe, but you feel it.”

Alonso staying at Aston Martin 'a strong signal' – Krack

A P8 is not much to get excited about for a guy who has seen and done so much, but Alonso himself admitted that in the context of 2026 Sepang was a welcome result.

“Obviously still far away from what we want to achieve,” said the two-time World Champion. “But to be in the points and to have a competitive pace in the race, it was encouraging.

“The whole weekend was a bit better, but it's still what it is. And this year has been painful and still a little bit struggling with the pace and the speed and the straights.

“So yeah, let's see. I think it's going to be circuit dependent. Probably this weekend we could be a little bit in the mix. Some others we will be right at the back. So we need to maximise the good weekends.”

Alonso is adamant that the AMR26 hasn’t got any better – it just worked well at Sepang relative to the competition.

“The car was exactly the same, physically the same, set-up the same, power unit same,” he said. “Everything was the same as Baku five days before Malaysia, and the performance difference was huge.

"So it's not about experimenting with the set-up, or having the car more in the window, or something that we can do on track.

“Unfortunately, it depends so much on the layout and the straights we have on that weekend. So as I said, probably this weekend is a good opportunity.”

Lance Stroll, who made Q2 for the first time at Sepang, also believes that Singapore will be a better weekend for the Aston-Honda package.

“I think so,” said the Canadian. “It's still straights, so we're still going to lose some time on the straights. But yeah, generally a lot more corners than long straights. So on paper, it's good for us.”

And does he agree with Krack’s suggestion that the good showing in Malaysia brought relief to the team?

“It's a temporary relief,” he said. “I think this week will probably be better again. But then we're going to go to the long straights and probably again lose two seconds in engine and stuff like that in the Mexicos and the Austins, and all those places.

title: How Albon navigates the realities of life on the road in F1
excerpt:
Between the Azerbaijan Grand Prix and the final race of the season, Alex Albon expects to spend only five days at his home in Monaco. For much of the rest of the year, he says, he will be living out of a suitcase.

This week, Formula 1 reaches the final stop of a triple-header that began in Baku before moving to Malaysia and then Singapore across three consecutive race weekends.

Along the way, the paddock has moved four hours ahead from Azerbaijan to Southeast Asia, as well as between very different climates and race schedules. Malaysia and Singapore may share the same time zone but, after a daytime race at Sepang, Singapore’s sessions take place much later as part of its famous night race.

After seven years in the world of F1, Williams driver Alex Albon has plenty of experience managing the travel that comes with the calendar. Speaking to F1.com in Baku at the start of the triple-header, however, he explained that the travel has never quite become second nature.

“No, it does feel like a lot,” he says when asked whether he ever gets used to stretches like this. “There’s the time zone shifting, which obviously we all have to deal with, and then there’s the physicality of the races themselves, which makes a big difference.

“Malaysia and Singapore are the two most physical tracks we have of the year, and they’re back-to-back, so that’s going to be a real challenge for us.

“On top of that, we’re shifting time zones between Malaysia and Singapore. Even though they are an hour’s flight away, because one is a night race and one is a day race, it’s around eight hours of time zone shifting that you need to do.”

Much of Albon’s schedule is therefore planned long before he arrives at the circuit. His manager works with Williams around team, partner and travel commitments, while his own plans after Singapore include another stop in Thailand.

“I spend every year trying to optimise my travel and my energy levels,” he explains. “You can’t imagine how much time my manager spends on scheduling and speaking with the team.

“We have partners that we need to fulfil [commitments for], and because of my Thai background, I’m going to Thailand after Singapore as well, so it does become busy.”

Living out of a suitcase

The amount of time Albon spends travelling becomes particularly clear when looking at the remainder of his season.

“From now until the last race of the year, I’ll spend five days in Monaco at home,” he admits. “During the second half of the season, I pretty much live in a suitcase. It is weird to think about.

“We travel with a big suitcase where you have to be prepared for cold weather, hot weather, all that stuff. Honestly, I buy things on the road, whether it’s underwear, socks or plain shirts, just to keep ticking over.”

When asked whether he ever unpacks, he laughs: "No, I'm the opposite! We try to fly in as late as we can. Even when we go back to Europe, we’re often returning to the UK for simulator work or marketing days with the team.

“By the time we leave again, it’s normally Wednesday night, or even Thursday morning for a European race. I don’t spend much time in the hotel. When we arrive, I go straight to bed, wake up and leave for the track.

“Instead, I have a couple of things from home that make the place feel a little more comfortable. I have an oil diffuser, my iPad, and I have a chair.

“It sounds really weird to say, but I have a chair that helps promote sleep, and I take that around with me as well.”

Turning jet lag into a ‘fine art’

That chair is only one part of the work Albon puts into his sleep.

Singapore presents a slightly different example. There is no official time difference from Malaysia, but the later schedule means the drivers shift their sleeping and eating patterns to fit around the night-time running.

Albon works with a sleep doctor alongside his nutritionist, although with seven seasons of F1 experience behind him, he says he has developed a good understanding of what works for him.

“At this point in my career, I don’t need much help," he says. "I know what I need to do.

“I have blue-light glasses, caffeine gum and eye masks. I don’t like using sleeping supplements, so I use natural tart cherry extract. That helps promote melatonin and helps you go to sleep naturally.

“It’s become a fine art. I usually start time zone shifting two or three days before I fly out, so that by the time I arrive at the track, I’m somewhat sensible.”

The Boy's Trip: Karting chaos, cycling tours and chess

Missing the routine of home

There are some things, however, that he cannot pack into a suitcase.

“I miss routine. I miss being normal, to be honest with you,” he admits when asked what he misses the most after spending long periods away. “When I’m on the road, we’ll be at a race a lot of the time. If we’ve got triple-headers, we fly on the Sunday night and arrive on the Monday.

“I do it, but it’s not always that spontaneous to walk around the city, grab a coffee or get lunch. I don’t get recognised that often, but during a race weekend you get recognised a lot more, so it’s harder to do the normal things. Those are the things I miss.

“I enjoy being at home, not doing much. Hotel rooms can feel quite cabin fever-esque as well, so you do struggle with that.

“I try to get outdoors and do training, but I miss the routine of waking up in my own bed, going to the same gym, going to my coffee shop, that sort of thing.”

While Albon’s home is in Monaco, he has made it easier to see his family and his many pets when he is back in the UK by getting a place closer to Williams’ Grove base.

“I don’t see my family all that much, unfortunately, and they’re the ones who have all the cats as well,” he explains.

“I try to make an effort... Before, I wouldn’t even go back to my family house before simulator work, so I would almost never see them. This year, having them closer by has given me the chance to see them a lot more, which has been a small game-changer.”

Finding routine through food

A passion for food is one part of travelling that Albon has increasingly begun to share with fans.

Alongside his partner, professional golfer Lily Muni He, Albon has started sharing a series called Al-bon Appétit this season, filming visits to restaurants during race weeks around the world and posting them on social media.

“Food is definitely synonymous with Asian culture, you’ll be hard-pressed to find an Asian who doesn’t like food!” he jokes.

“It brings a bit of routine too. On Wednesday nights, sometimes Thursdays, we’ll find a restaurant in the city. We’ll find a small place that’s famous for something, or somewhere we know has really good food, and we thought, ‘Why not film it since we’re doing it anyway?’

“Giovanni [Moioli], who’s behind the camera, is a super nice guy and he makes it feel natural. It pretty much is the three of us having dinner.

“It’s nice not to be ordering room service. I know there are a lot of drivers who spend their whole time in the hotel room, whereas I like to get out there as much as I can.

"I think some of the other drivers are too famous. They have no chance!”

Why Albon and Williams have decided to stick rather than twist

Travelling with Williams

Albon is only one part of a much larger Williams group moving around the calendar.

Asked whether having the same team travelling with him can make it feel like a second home, his answer is slightly different to what might be expected.

“It’s possibly more different than you realise. It’s actually quite disconnected in many ways,” he explains. “I feel for the team because, if you think about the big picture, I talk about my struggles and it’s a little bit like I’m playing the violin.

“The staff, especially the race team, are doing the same amount of air miles as I am, yet they’re not able to fly the way we are or stay in as nice a hotel as we are.

“A lot of them are older than I am and a lot of them have families, children. It’s tough. It’s really tough to be on the road.

“I respect a lot of the Formula 1 personnel for doing this. Some of them do it for 20 years. It’s a really difficult lifestyle.”

The travelling team do not necessarily spend every evening together, but Albon says there are conscious efforts throughout the season to create opportunities away from the circuit.

“We don’t spend as much time together on the road as you would think,” he admits. “However, it’s a conscious effort to make sure that when we are together, we’ll have a good dinner or do something to show appreciation.

“When we go to Austin, Mexico and Brazil, we’ll make sure the drivers do an event. We had one in Madrid at Carlos [Sainz]’s family track, and that was a lot of fun.

“These moments where we’re all together on the road and doing some form of activity, it does make you feel like a big family.”

title: George Russell confirms double punishment blow after agonising Mercedes failure
excerpt:
George Russell faces two grid penalties for changing a power unit in the remaining seven races, starting this weekend in Singapore.

George Russell has confirmed he will take a second grid penalty before the end of the season, on top of the one he faces this weekend at the Singapore Grand Prix, after his Mercedes engine failed in the closing stages in Sepang.

Russell retired with a power unit failure in the closing laps of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, ending a race in which teammate Kimi Antonelli finished second.

The unit that failed is now being replaced, triggering a grid penalty at Marina Bay, but Russell has revealed that a further change, and another penalty, is now unavoidable later in the campaign.

Speaking to select media including RacingNews365 on Singapore media day, Russell explained that the engine which failed was not actually overdue for retirement.

Asked whether the failure was caused by the power unit being used for too long, the Briton was unequivocal.

"No, the engine wasn't stretched too long," said Russell. "It was the sixth race of the engine, and obviously you have four engines a year, six races per engine when you split it up.

"We actually put that engine in on Sunday in Budapest, so it was actually the sixth race, but minus qualifying and the practice sessions of Budapest."

Driver

George Russell

British

63

George Russell reveals Mercedes' engine change delay hope

Russell said Mercedes had been trying to delay a penalty until it could fit an upgraded unit built under the FIA's Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities mechanism, which the Brackley-based squad qualified for after its engine trailed Red Bull's on the official performance index.

"We were waiting to take the engine penalty with the ADUO update, but obviously, unfortunately, we've had to take it here [in Singapore]," added Russell.

"But with seven races remaining, that's longer than the engines are designed for. Unfortunately, it means I'll be taking another penalty at some point between the next race and the end of the season, so yeah, feels a little bit like one thing after another right now.

"But that's just how the cookie crumbles."

title: Lewis Hamilton bemoans FIA and young F1 drivers over wet-weather caution
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton feels F1's current wet-weather approach is overly cautious, pointing the finger at both FIA race control and the younger generation of drivers.

Hamilton finished third in Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, climbing from 18th early on after starting on slicks to the podium behind race winner Max Verstappen and Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli.

Heavy rain before the race began triggered a 40-minute delay. The event eventually commenced behind the safety car for what was meant to be two formation laps, and a possible standing start.

That did not materialise, however, due to a software 'bug that infected several systems, including that of Hamilton in his Ferrari. He had to stop on track, and reboot the SF-26 to get going again.

Hamilton, who started that race on the front row alongside polesitter Verstappen, said he had been relishing the prospect of wheel-to-wheel battles in the rain, only to see the opportunity disappear.

"I was looking forward to a wet race," said Hamilton, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365. "When it started raining, I was like, 'Oh yeah, this is going to be fun.

"We did the laps to the grid, and there was obviously a lot of spray, and then with all the delay and everything like that, ultimately I didn't get to have that battle that I wanted to have with Max, which I was excited about, and Kimi."

[Article continues below]

The seven-time F1 champion, who has spoken previously about his affection for driving in treacherous conditions, drew a direct comparison with his early career, when Bridgestone's rain tyres were developed through far greater on-track mileage than today's Pirelli compounds.

"Wet weather races aren't the same as we used to have," Hamilton said. "I've had great races in the rain, like 2008 [his British GP victory]. Ultimately, we had more testing back then.

"We had better tyres for the rain because we were able to...I guess they were developed more with Bridgestone back in the day.

"And I love racing in the rain, personally."

Taking umbrage with some of the decisions that are made when it comes to racing in the wet, Hamilton added: "I do think the guys running the show [in FIA race control] are more and more and more cautious, but then again, the young drivers coming in are more and more cautious.

"Us old-school drivers are like, 'Let's get racing', and the youngsters are like, 'Let's not race'.

"So they [FIA race control] are getting two different bits of information, and they are super cautious as well.

"Whereas I'm like, 'Let's get going' under extreme conditions, because that's where we really get to test ourselves.

"Is it more risky? Absolutely. When I was on the slick tyre [in Malaysia], it was the trickiest conditions. It's wet, and I'm on slicks. But I love that challenge, and that's what racing is, where you have to drive by the seat of your pants.

"That's really where you can make the difference, and ultimately, that is where I did make the difference at the end of the day."

title: Why F1 will make bizarre Singapore Grand Prix history this weekend
excerpt:
Formula 1 will make history at Marina Bay this weekend when Saturday's Sprint race becomes the first competitive session in Singapore Grand Prix history to be held in daylight rather than under floodlights.

Every grand prix held in Singapore since the event's debut in 2008 has taken place at night, with Marina Bay serving as F1's first-ever night race.

That remains the case for this weekend's main grand prix, which is still scheduled for its traditional evening slot.

But the sprint, set for 17:00 local time on Saturday, will run in daylight before darkness falls for qualifying later that evening.

The scheduling quirk stems from the need for a mandatory four-hour buffer between the start of the sprint and the night qualifying session that follows, while also allowing support categories to run their own events in Marina Bay's evening prime-time slot.

Lando Norris addresses unusual Singapore GP Sprint

Lando Norris does not expect the unusual timing to have much bearing on performance, telling select media, including RacingNews365, that Singapore's climate stays largely consistent whatever the hour.

"I don't think it changes too much, honestly, because it's not like it gets a lot colder or warmer depending on the time," said the McLaren driver.

"It's just always pretty hot here. So here, not so much [of a difference]. I think in other places, Bahrain, for example, it can be quite the opposite.

"During the day, it's horrible in terms of the effect the temperature has, and in the evenings, the track gets a lot quicker, the car works worse, all of those things. So there's a big effect. Here, I think it's quite a bit smaller, and it's just more consistent."

"So, honestly, I'm going to go with I don't think there's too much of a difference between it. It's just visually things look different, but that's really the main thing."

Norris's comments echo the technical picture around Marina Bay's unusual conditions. Track temperatures at the street circuit are driven far more by the presence or absence of direct sunlight than by swings in the ambient air, which stays roughly stable between day and night due to Singapore's near-equatorial location.

That is markedly different to a venue like Bahrain, where desert night races produce a sharp drop in air temperature once the sun sets, fundamentally altering tyre behaviour and track grip.

Teams are expected to treat Saturday's daytime sprint running with some caution when it comes to setup relevance, given that hotter asphalt and a dirtier track surface in sunlight typically behave differently to the cooler, more rubbered-in conditions under the floodlights come qualifying and the race itself.

title: Lance Stroll explains reason behind 'f*** this s***' Aston Martin radio message
excerpt:
A radio message from Lance Stroll went semi-viral following the Bahrain GP, with the Aston Martin driver having revealed what was actually being discussed.

Lance Stroll has explained that the frustrated radio outburst he sent during the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was rooted in tyre management, not a mechanical complaint.

The Aston Martin driver finished 12th at the Sepang International Circuit, more than 18 seconds behind race winner Max Verstappen, after a weekend in which the team's approach to tyre conservation appeared to backfire.

During the grand prix, Stroll responded to a radio message by saying "f*** this s***", before overtaking Haas' Esteban Ocon moments later.

Stroll said the team had been managing its tyres on the assumption it would be a demanding stint, only to discover the Pirellis were holding up far better than expected, costing him track position before deciding to attack again.

Addressing the radio message, Stroll told select media, including RacingNews365: "That was more [about] tyres. We were trying to manage the tyres, and then the more we were managing the tyres, we were just losing temperature and falling out of the window.

"And it was actually not a management race. It was a flat out race. So, and then when we started pushing, started overtaking some cars, and you know, I think that probably cost us some points in the last race, just over management and not pushing the tyres.

"I think it was that the tyres were a lot more robust than than we thought it would be."

Driver

Lance Stroll

Canadian

18

Stroll warns Aston Martin current form only a 'temporary relief'

Attention has now turned to the Singapore Grand Prix and the Marina Bay Street Circuit, a layout dominated by low-speed corners and short acceleration zones that typically masks the power deficit Aston Martin has struggled with all season.

Stroll believes it offers a brief window where the car's strengths can shine through, before the calendar swings back to circuits that expose Honda's straight-line shortfall.

Asked about Aston Martin's recent upturn in form, the Canadian was cautious about reading too much into it.

"It's a temporary relief," said Stroll on Aston Martin's recent form. "I think this last week, this week will probably be better again, but then we're going to go to the long straights and probably again lose two seconds of engine and stuff like that in the Mexicos and the Austins and all those places.

"So, yeah, try and capitalise on these weekends where we know it's more about the car and less about the engine, and then in the background we just have to keep pushing hard for a lot more power and all the stuff we know we need to work on."

title: Esteban Ocon confirms plan for F1 career after Haas departure
excerpt:
Esteban Ocon has confirmed he has no intention of being present in any race paddock other than F1 next year, even if it means he will be without a race seat.

Haas and Ocon confirmed at the end of September that they would part ways at the end of the 2026 campaign.

With very few seats remaining on the 2027 grid, Ocon's options for a full-time drive in F1 next year appear to be limited.

But when asked where he could take his talents next season, speaking to the media including RacingNews365, Ocon replied: “F1.

“That's where I deserve to be, if I look at the results and what I've shown in F1. I deserve to be in F1.

“Of course, there are other categories which are fantastic as well. But I want to be racing in F1 for the next five to seven years.

“That's where I want to be, so I will keep pushing to be in that position. In the near future, that's the only thing I'm looking at so far.”

When asked if he would race even if he didn't obtain an F1 drive, Ocon stated: “No.”

Ocon insisted that he will stick around in F1 in any circumstance, even if it means he will not get to race in other categories.

Should he fail to sign for a full-time seat for 2027, Ocon insisted it would mean taking on a third driver role.

“Yes. If there are no possibilities to race next year, that's what I will do.”

A third driver role is something Ocon is no stranger to, having performed the duties at Mercedes in 2019 before joining Renault the following year.

title: Sergio Perez highlights 'tension' for Cadillac at 'last chance' Singapore weekend
excerpt:
Sergio Perez enters the Singapore Grand Prix as a race winner at the track, as he looks to produce another strong result - this time for Cadillac.

Sergio Perez has labelled the Singapore Grand Prix as Cadillac's "last chance" to get itself into the points-scoring positions this year.

The sport's newest team has endured a challenging campaign thus far and has not yet bagged a championship point as it continues to get up to speed in F1.

With Singapore being one of the more challenging circuits on the calendar, drivers are facing added peril with just one practice session taking place before the competitive sessions.

Perez, who is a race winner around the Marina Bay Circuit, is hopeful Cadillac can finally get itself on the scoresheet this weekend.

"It's a good opportunity for us," Perez told media including RacingNews365.

"Probably our last one to do something important, given the delta we currently have with the car and that we are not bringing anything.

"It's probably our last good chance to try and get a strong result here. That will be a crucial one for us."

Driver

Sergio Pérez

Mexican

11

Perez hints at Cadillac risk in Singapore

The Singapore weekend is the final sprint event of the year, giving teams two bites of the cherry to score points.

As Cadillac aims to bag its best result yet, Pérez suggested it will take added risk during the weekend to walk away rewarded.

"It [the sprint format] puts a little bit more uncertainty on the weekend, a little bit more tension," Pérez added.

"On a street circuit, at a race that is so hard to get the confidence [to] build up, the driver can make a bit of a difference in these sort of weekends.

"Normally on a circuit, it takes you a bit of time to get up to speed. So, one practice into qualifying, it's good.

"We will give everything we have. We have to, especially for qualifying, we need to be able to overdeliver massively to get something.

"Baku was a good example. Hopefully, here can be a bit of the same."

title: Fernando Alonso clarifies 2027 racing plans after intense speculation
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso was heavily linked with an entry into the 2027 Dakar Rally over the last week.

Fernando Alonso has denied that he will take part in the Dakar Rally early next year, prior to the start of the 2027 F1 season.

Earlier this week, various media reports stated that Alonso was set to enter the event for the second time in his career, having already competed in the famous event in 2020.

Having committed himself to an Aston Martin F1 drive for 2027, Alonso hinted that there were "more surprises" coming regarding his short-term future.

However, it seems that this will not be an outing at Dakar, as he insisted the two-week event would significantly disrupt his preparations for the new F1 season.

"I read those rumours," Alonso told media including RacingNews365.

"But no, I don't think it's possible physically.

"It's nearly impossible to fit in demanding programmes like an F1 championship and Dakar."

[Article continues below]

Alonso denies GT3 adventure

Alonso's last entry at Dakar came during his break away from the sport, meaning he did not have to prioritise his readiness for F1 while battling for the win.

But as to what the "surprises" could be going forward, Alonso also moved to rule out GT3 racing, a class that Max Verstappen has dipped his toes into across the last year.

"Not GT3, I never tried," Alonso said. "It needs a very big preparation.

"Every one of these challenges, because they were good or less competitive in the past, people think that they are easy.

"So it requires a lot of preparation, a lot of determination, a lot of luck to succeed.

"So when I do the next challenge, I will announce it, it will not be a rumour. It will be myself doing it.

"It will be because I think there is enough preparation and enough of a risk to take."

title: Aston Martin to be 'glued to the TV' as Fernando Alonso Dakar speculation grows
excerpt:
Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack has admitted he would be keen to see Fernando Alonso compete in other motorsport categories alongside his F1 duties.

Alonso put speculation over his F1 future to bed last week when he declared he had extended his commitment to Aston Martin.

However, the two-time champion teased that there were "more surprises" on the way before speculation increased that he could enter the Dakar Rally, having already done so in 2020.

The situation was put to Krack ahead of the Singapore Grand Prix weekend, who insisted he is unopposed to Alonso taking on such challenges.

"We had Robert [Kubica] doing rally, we had Kimi [Raikkonen] doing rally, we had Max [Verstappen] doing GT3, we had Lance [Stroll] doing GT3," Krack told media including RacingNews365.

"I personally like that. It is good for motorsport in general if the drivers do that.

"What happens, I cannot really say in Fernando's case for next year.

"But generally, it is a very good thing, and it also shows what racing approach or what racers they are.

"With the calendar we have, they want to do other things. For Max, it was seven weekends in a row with all the GT3 stuff.

"It shows what racers they are, and it will glue me to the TV as well, like all of us."

Krack addresses Le Mans possibility for Alonso

Next year, there will be no clash between the 24 Hours of Le Mans and a grand prix, opening the door for F1 drivers to take part in the iconic race.

Alonso, who is a two-time winner of the race, has long been linked with a future entry to the race in a partnership with fellow F1 champion Verstappen.

However, the Spaniard has already stated he does not expect such a collaboration to occur in 2027.

When asked if Aston Martin would allow its drivers to race at Le Mans, Krack added: "I'm not making this final approval, 'yes or no, you are allowed to'.

"So I can't really confirm. I'm just saying personally, this is a good thing because race drivers should race."

title: Valtteri Bottas reveals 'jungle mind games' on 'epic' journey to Singapore
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas has delivered an insight into his "epic" journey that he undertook travelling from Malaysia to Singapore this weekend.

After the race weekend in Sepang, rather than do the usual commute of travelling by plane, Bottas opted to cycle the journey.

On Sunday after the grand prix in Malaysia, Bottas cycled 56 kilometres from the track to Port Dickson.

However, Monday and Tuesday marked the biggest legs of his journey as he cycled 322 km across both days, arriving in Johor Bahru on Tuesday evening.

He then completed the final leg of 40km to Singapore on Wednesday.

The unusual nature of the journey captured attention ahead of this weekend's race in Singapore, which is considered to be the greatest physical test the drivers face all season due to the heat and humidity.

Bottas insisted the journey was thoroughly planned to ensure he would not be exhausted by the time it came to drive his Cadillac F1 car again.

"I obviously wouldn't do it if I knew it would hurt my performance," Bottas told media including RacingNews365.

"The amount of sweat in those days was quite impressive. But definitely, you get used to the heat. So that can help me, hopefully a little bit.

"I think Tiffany mentioned it as a joke, 'hey, you could just ride from there, it's not that far'.

"Then I was like, 'Hmm, maybe I could'. I obviously had to check the distance, how the roads are, the timings, and then just made a solid plan for each day.

"All the routes were planned. I also planned that the two bigger days were Monday and Tuesday, so they're not too close to the race weekend.

"If I did a big day on, let's say, Wednesday, then that could already compromise my Friday in terms of recovery.

"Yesterday ended up being a short ride, a recovery ride. Today I can have an easy day."

[Article continues below]

Bottas reveals run-ins with wildlife during cycle

Bottas' unique journey also saw him ride through the darkness and through some regions of jungle, adding a mental challenge to the physical one.

The ride did not come without its perils, as Bottas had to navigate some of the local wildlife en route to the Marina Bay Circuit.

"I saw some snakes, which I was a little bit worried about, but actually they were pretty chill. They were just doing their thing," he said.

"I saw one cobra, one python just crossing the path in front of me. I saw some of those big lizards that you also see here [in Singapore], one was on the path.

"I had to jump over it on a bike because I saw it last minute. I got chased by one dog, I got stuck behind a group of cows on one small track.

"Eventually they moved away. The wildest part was the riding at night in the jungle. The noise in there, your mind starts to play games.

"'What is out there? Who knows what is out there?' But then you just need to crack on and keep going.

"Riding with your lights at night, that was probably the most epic part in the forest."

Bottas commended the Malaysian and Singapore locals for their attitude towards his journey, revealing he was recognised on some parts of the ride.

"I did have some road sections, but as much as possible was off-road," he said.

"Even the locals, the cars, they were really polite. They always would leave lots of space.

"Once the news started to break that I'm actually doing it, there were some locals who recognised me, cheering me on, which was cool."

title: FIA reveal findings after review into Sepang formation lap bug
excerpt:
The formation lap at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia saw drama with several cars coming to a stop on the track.

The FIA has concluded its review into the formation lap incident at the Bahrain Grand Prix, held at the Sepang International Circuit in Malaysia, attributing the issue to a "software bug".

The governing body opened its probe after the formation lap was disrupted during the event, which took place at Sepang rather than Bahrain's usual home circuit as part of this year's calendar.

Following a delay due to wet weather, the formation lap got underway some 40 minutes after the scheduled start.

However, several cars ran into issues when running at low speed, with some even coming to a complete stop on the circuit due to power unit problems.

It resulted in a further delay to the start of the race while the FIA diagnosed the issue and implemented a fix across the grid.

After the race, it announced that it was conducting a review, which it has now revealed focused on four key areas. They were;

The precise cause of the loss of power experienced by a number of cars on the formation lap

Measures that can be introduced to mitigate a recurrence of the same issues

The future management of wet-weather Power Unit settings (energy limit restraints)

Learnings from the data from individual team and Power Unit manufacturers

[Article continues below]

FIA confirm change for US Grand Prix in Austin

Having assessed the situation, the FIA has detailed that should similar conditions occur this weekend in Singapore, the power units will revert to the configurations used in Malaysia.

For the round that follows Singapore in the USA, the FIA has promised to introduce a further update to the wet-weather software.

In a statement, the sport's governing body stated: “The review also recommended that measures would be implemented for testing of the software, recognising that opportunities for testing are limited, to make it robust as possible.

“The FIA, together with the teams and Power Unit Manufacturers (PUMs), will continue to strengthen Power Unit software testing and verification capabilities, enhancing the overall validation process through independent assessment and collaborative feedback, including input from the supplier of the standardised Electronics Control Unit (ECU).”

After the race, the FIA's single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis declared that the software was not tested in such conditions as seen in Malaysia.

The FIA has clarified that comment, stating: “The FIA would like to address comments suggesting that the software had not been tested prior to its deployment.

“Before implementation, teams and Power Unit manufacturers conducted simulation exercises to validate the software package, which was subsequently tested in full-scale running during Free Practice 1 sessions at both the Belgian Grand Prix and the Dutch Grand Prix.

title: Max Verstappen weighs in on Christian Horner absence: 'It's less stressful'
excerpt:
Christian Horner departed his role as Red Bull team boss midway through the 2025 F1 season.

Max Verstappen has admitted that the F1 paddock is "less stressful" without the presence of Christian Horner.

Horner was the long-time team boss at Red Bull, taking on the role when the team formed on the grid in 2005, becoming the sport's youngest team principal at the time.

He stayed in the position for 20 years but exited the team midway through the 2025 campaign amid a difficult run of form for Red Bull.

Horner was one of the sport's biggest personalities outside of the drivers and was undaunted from playing the political game with his fellow team leaders.

But Verstappen admitted it is not the approach he is fond of.

"To be honest, I like to see that people get on. It is not nice when you constantly have tension between people," Verstappen told PA.

"Of course, from the outside, people like it, but honestly between the teams, it is better when you have just a friendly relationship.

"It is not as spicy, but I obviously quite like how things are going at the moment, with everyone's behaviour, let's put it like that.

"It is less stressful. We are all leading a stressful life and, when you can take a bit of stress out of it at times, it is good."

title: FIA declare Singapore heat hazard as drivers prepare for biggest test
excerpt:
Round 17 of the 2026 F1 season sees the sport descend upon the Marina Bay Circuit, host of the Singapore Grand Prix.

The FIA has declared a heat hazard for this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, triggering mandatory cooling measures for every team on the Marina Bay Street Circuit grid.

The declaration falls under Article B1.5.10 of the FIA Sporting Regulations, which comes into effect whenever the official weather service forecasts a heat index above 31.0°C during a race weekend session.

Singapore's notoriously muggy night-race conditions have pushed forecasts past that threshold.

With the hazard confirmed, teams must fit functional Driver Cooling System hardware to their cars. The protocol also adjusts the minimum weight limits, adding 2kg during practice and qualifying and 5kg for the race itself to account for the extra equipment.

Drivers who choose not to wear the cooling vest must instead carry 0.5kg of compensating ballast in the cockpit, a route Mercedes has taken at previous heat-hazard rounds this year, having determined that running its system reliably across a full race distance was not viable without diverting resources from car development.

Singapore is often considered the single biggest physical challenge on the F1 calendar, and the numbers behind that reputation are stark.

Marina Bay's tropical climate exposes drivers to ambient air temperatures above 30°C alongside humidity typically ranging between 70 and 90 per cent, which severely restricts the body's natural ability to cool itself through sweat.

Drivers can lose up to three to four kilograms of body fluid over the course of the race.

Singapore heat hazard not an isolated case

Singapore is far from an isolated case this season.

The FIA previously declared heat hazards for the Austrian Grand Prix at the Red Bull Ring in June, when a European heatwave pushed ambient temperatures to 33°C, and for the Italian Grand Prix at Monza in September, where air temperatures climbed into the mid-30s.

Most recently, the hazard was invoked for the Bahrain Grand Prix at Sepang, where tropical humidity made conditions feel close to 35°C.

The cooling mandate traces back to the 2023 Qatar Grand Prix, when cockpit temperatures exceeded 50°C and several drivers suffered acute distress, including Logan Sargeant's retirement through dehydration and Alex Albon's hospital visit.
